Bathroom Fitting Ideas for Small Bathrooms

30 July 2026·BMB Renovation

A small bathroom does not have to feel cramped or difficult to use. The right layout, carefully chosen fittings and well-planned storage can make a compact room feel calmer, brighter and more practical. Whether you are updating a cloakroom, refurbishing an en-suite or redesigning a family bathroom, the best results usually come from considering how every centimetre will be used before choosing tiles or taps. These bathroom fitting ideas for small bathrooms are suitable for many UK homes, including properties where awkward corners, narrow rooms and limited natural light create additional challenges.

Start with the layout, not the fittings

Before selecting a basin or shower, measure the room carefully and mark the position of the door, window, soil pipe, radiator and existing water connections. Think about the clear space needed to open the door, sit comfortably on the toilet and step into the shower. A layout that looks good on paper may feel restrictive if several doors or drawers open into the same area. In some rooms, reversing the door swing or using a sliding or folding door can release valuable floor space, although the best option depends on the property and existing structure. Keeping the toilet and basin near their current plumbing positions may also help control the scope of the work, while moving fixtures can create a much better arrangement where the existing layout is particularly inefficient.

Layouts that often work well in compact bathrooms

  • A wall-hung or compact close-coupled toilet placed in a corner can leave a clearer route through the room.
  • A corner basin can work well in a cloakroom, especially where a standard basin would interfere with the door.
  • A walk-in shower or shower enclosure at the far end of a narrow room can make the space feel more open than a bath with a bulky screen.
  • A shower-bath can provide bathing flexibility where the household needs a bath but the room cannot accommodate separate fixtures.
  • A sliding shower door or inward-folding enclosure can avoid the projecting door swing associated with some framed shower units.
  • A bath installed along the longest wall may be the most practical choice, with a wall-mounted toilet or basin helping to preserve visible floor area.

Choose compact fittings without sacrificing comfort

Small fittings are useful, but the narrowest product is not automatically the best choice. A basin that is too shallow may cause splashing, while an undersized shower can be uncomfortable for everyday use. Look for proportions that suit the room and the people using it. Short-projection toilets, slim vanity units and compact baths can reduce obstruction without making the bathroom feel improvised. Wall-hung furniture and toilets can also create a more continuous floor line, making cleaning easier and helping the room appear less crowded. Concealed cisterns may provide a neat finish, but they need suitable access for maintenance, so the installation should be planned rather than boxed in without thought.

Use walls and corners for storage

In a small bathroom, storage should use vertical space wherever possible. A mirrored cabinet above the basin can combine everyday storage with the function of a mirror. Recessed shower niches can hold shampoo and soap without introducing a shelf that projects into the enclosure, provided the wall construction allows one to be formed properly. Tall, narrow cupboards can use an otherwise overlooked strip beside a basin or toilet. Open shelving is helpful for towels and attractive accessories, but too much visible storage can make a compact room look untidy. A vanity unit with drawers often gives easier access than a cupboard, while wall-mounted units keep more of the floor visible.

  • Plan a dedicated place for toilet rolls, cleaning products, towels and spare toiletries before finalising the furniture.
  • Use hooks on the back of the door or on an unused wall for towels and dressing gowns.
  • Consider a heated towel rail that suits the available wall width rather than allowing a large radiator to dominate the room.
  • Keep frequently used items within reach and store occasional-use products in taller or less accessible cupboards.
  • Avoid filling every wall with shelves; a small room benefits from a controlled number of storage zones.

Make a small bathroom feel larger

Light, continuity and visual simplicity can have a noticeable effect on how spacious a bathroom feels. Large-format tiles may reduce the number of grout lines, although they still need to be suitable for the wall dimensions and installed on an appropriately prepared surface. Pale wall colours, a consistent floor finish and clear glass shower panels can help maintain an uninterrupted view across the room. Gloss finishes reflect light, while matt surfaces can give a softer appearance and may be easier to live with depending on the product. A well-placed mirror can reflect light and increase the sense of depth, but it should be positioned for practical use rather than purely for visual effect. Good layered lighting is also important: ambient lighting, task lighting around the mirror and suitable illumination in the shower area should be designed with the room and installation requirements in mind.

Why professional planning matters

A compact bathroom leaves little room for errors. Uneven walls, concealed pipework, floor levels, ventilation and the position of electrical equipment can all affect which layout is achievable. A professional renovation company can assess the room, coordinate the fitting sequence and identify clashes before installation begins. This is especially useful when the project involves several trades, such as plumbing, tiling, electrical work and cabinet installation. It is worth discussing practical details early, including whether the existing soil pipe can remain, where new pipework will run, how access panels will be provided and what type of ventilation the room requires. Your contractor should also explain which finishes are suitable for wet areas and how the work will be sequenced. A clear plan helps avoid choosing a basin that cannot be opened properly, a shower screen that blocks a towel rail or storage that prevents access to essential services. Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best layout for a very small bathroom?+
The best layout depends on the room shape, door, window and existing plumbing. Common solutions include a corner basin, short-projection toilet, compact shower and wall-mounted storage.
Is a shower better than a bath in a small bathroom?+
A shower usually uses less floor space, but a shower-bath can be a practical compromise if your household needs bathing facilities. The choice depends on the room dimensions and how the bathroom is used.
How can I add storage to a small bathroom?+
Use vertical and recessed space with a mirrored cabinet, tall cupboard, vanity drawers, shower niche and wall hooks. Plan storage for towels and cleaning products before choosing the fittings.
Can a professional make a small bathroom feel bigger?+
Yes. Careful positioning of fittings, clear shower screens, continuous finishes, suitable lighting and well-planned storage can improve both the practical use and visual spaciousness of the room.
